posts:
Private surveillance vendor Flock Safety funds local politicians while seeking municipal license plate camera contracts.
Evidence: Safety claims, Vendor donations, Pay-to-play risk
#Aletheia #Surveillance 🌐

Flock Safety frames license plate readers as essential public safety infrastructure, while municipal officials maintain political donations do not influence purchasing decisions.
Stated Judgement: (+0.57, +0.37) — Greater Good

Election records reveal Flock Safety directs campaign cash directly to local leaders overseeing public safety contracts, blending private corporate expansion with municipal power.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.18, +0.22) — Greatest Lie

Verdict: FAIL — Fall into Deception.
Flock Safety uses corporate campaign cash to secure local vendor lock-in, replacing objective procurement with political pay-to-play.

Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 11.5, z: 2)

- Flock Safety: FAIL (-0.65, +0.45) — Pay-to-play campaign cash.
- Cicero Officials: FAIL (-0.60, -0.40) — Taking vendor funds.
- Chicago Sun-Times: PASS (+0.70, +0.60) — Exposing municipal cash.
Flock Safety donated thousands to Cicero Town President Larry Dominick and other officials whose agencies operate its cameras, raising ethics concerns over government contracts.

The Bright Side:
Automatic license plate readers do help police solve crimes and locate stolen vehicles, proving high operational utility when deployed with strict independent civil oversight.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Flock claims to solve community crime (WHAT), but directs cash to politicians (WHO) to retain contracts, committing a Metaphysical Plane Error by swapping public safety for vendor retention.

Social Physics Analysis:
Flock executes a Smart Selfish Maneuver. They manufacture panic over crime to sell surveillance tech, then funnel revenue into campaign coffers to capture elected regulators and guarantee recurring municipal revenue.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Deception.
Modal Dynamics: will be -> Won't be via Red Top (The Imperial Trap).
Promising public safety while locking towns into private surveillance traps plots a trajectory straight into corporate extraction.

The Unavoidable Truth: Private vendors giving campaign cash to municipal contract buyers corrupts police tech procurement.

The Unavoidable Lie: Vendor campaign contributions have no bearing on municipal police contract renewals.

Alethekanon:
When security vendors fund the politicians who buy their equipment, surveillance ceases to be a public good and becomes a self-funding municipal cartel.

Awwthekanon:
Communities deserve real protection without having their privacy traded for campaign checks, leaving neighbors caught between local safety needs and backroom politics.

Brothekanon:
Selling cameras to cops and then writing checks to the mayor isn't public service, man—it's just classic pay-to-play wrapped in a high-tech bow.

Spirithekanon:
"No one can serve two masters." Matthew 6:24 FAIL
When vendor profits dictate civic safety decisions, public duty is sacrificed for money.

A Flock license plate reader on the Near West Side.

Candace Dane Chambers / Sun-Times

Share

Flock Safety license plate reading cameras have spread throughout the Chicago area, stirring controversy about surveillance and civil liberties while helping snare crooks.

The company’s money has also begun to spread to local politics, according to election records.

In Cicero, where Flock has a number of cameras monitoring traffic, the Atlanta company has given several campaign contributions to Town President Larry Dominick, who oversees public safety in the near west suburb.

The first contribution to the Cicero Voters Alliance (The Larry Dominick Team) was for $1,000, made in 2021, according to Illinois State Board of Elections records.

In 2022 another $1,000 arrived from Flock, while in 2024 the company gave $2,000.

In 2025, the year Dominick successfully ran for reelection, Flock gave him another $2,000.

The community now has 31 Flock cameras, and first engaged the company in or about 2020, a town spokesman said.

“The Town of Cicero is proud of the hundreds of crimes solved with the help of Flock cameras and our officers would be utilizing them to help keep the community safe with or without the $6,000 they’ve contributed to President Dominick over the last six years,” the spokesman said.
